summary: ZRTP lets two phones or softphones agree on a secret key for encrypting a call by doing a Diffie-Hellman exchange directly in the media stream, on the same port as the audio. It needs no certificates or help from the call-signaling protocol, and users can compare a short spoken code to catch a man-in-the-middle. It is an informational document, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Two friends on a call each mix a secret color into a shared paint, so both end up with the same color nobody else can guess. Then they read a short code aloud to check nobody sneaked in.

questions: how to encrypt voip media without certificates
what is the zrtp short authentication string
subtitle: Two endpoints agree on a secret key for encrypting a call inside the media stream itself, with no certificates and no help from call signaling.

tldr.problem: Encrypting a voice or video call needs both ends to share a key, but many approaches depend on a public key infrastructure, certificates or the signaling servers.
tldr.mechanism: ZRTP runs an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman exchange in the media path on the same port as RTP, then derives keys and salt for a Secure RTP (SRTP) session. Users compare a Short Authentication String aloud, and cached secrets give key continuity for later calls.
tldr.outcome: Calls get end-to-end keys without a PKI, and a man-in-the-middle can be spotted by the SAS or by a mismatch with cached secrets. The RFC is Informational, not a standard.

today: RFC 6189 is an Informational RFC published in April 2011. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata, so it remains the specification of ZRTP version 1.10.

sections.title: What ZRTP Is
sections.content:
ZRTP is a key agreement protocol. It performs a Diffie-Hellman key exchange during call setup, in the media path, over the same port as the RTP media stream that was set up by a signaling protocol such as SIP. The shared secret it produces is used to generate keys and salt for a Secure RTP (SRTP) session.

The RFC lists several design features. It uses a public key algorithm but does not rely on a public key infrastructure (PKI) and uses no persistent public keys. It uses ephemeral Diffie-Hellman with a hash commitment and lets users detect a man-in-the-middle (MiTM) by reading a short authentication string (SAS) aloud. It has Perfect Forward Secrecy, because keys are destroyed at the end of the call. Even if users skip the SAS, it caches key material for the next call, a form of key continuity like SSH. Everything is peer to peer, with no servers.

ZRTP can be used without any hint in the signaling, which gives a best-effort SRTP capability. If an SDP attribute a=zrtp-hash is sent, the media is bound to the signaling. ZRTP is designed for unicast sessions with a voice stream and, in terms of RTP topologies, for point-to-point only. Multiparty conferences use a separate ZRTP session between each party and the bridge.
sections.plainLanguage: ZRTP lets two phones invent a secret lock code in the middle of a call, with no helper in between. When the call ends, the code is thrown away.

sections.title: The Call Flow and Key Agreement Modes
sections.content:
ZRTP starts after the endpoints have negotiated an ordinary RTP session, and after ICE has finished if it is used. Both sides send a Hello message carrying the version, algorithm options and a ZID, a unique 96-bit random ID generated once at installation. A HelloACK answers each Hello. Then one side sends a Commit and becomes the initiator. In Diffie-Hellman mode the responder replies with DHPart1, the initiator sends DHPart2, both compute the SRTP keys, and Confirm1, Confirm2 and Conf2ACK finish the exchange before SRTP media begins.

There are three key agreement modes.

  • Diffie-Hellman mode makes a fresh shared secret and mixes in any cached secrets.
  • Preshared mode skips the DH calculation by reusing a cached secret, which helps slow processors or a quick restart of an interrupted session. It still has forward secrecy, but a passive wiretapper holding a captured cache could decrypt the next call if it is also in Preshared mode.
  • Multistream mode derives keys for extra streams, such as video added to a secure voice call, from an already active ZRTP session key. No second DH exchange is done and DHPart1 and DHPart2 are omitted.

Messages are retransmitted because RTP usually runs over lossy UDP. Hello uses timer T1, recommended at 50 ms, doubling up to 200 ms, for 20 tries. Other messages use T2, recommended at 150 ms, doubling up to 1200 ms, for 10 tries. Only the initiator retransmits Commit, DHPart2 and Confirm2.
sections.plainLanguage: First the phones say hello and compare what lock types they know. Then they swap secret ingredients, bake the same key, and check it works before talking privately.

sections.title: Negotiation and Commit Contention
sections.content:
Each endpoint sends its algorithms in order of preference in its Hello. For versions, this specification defines ZRTP version 1.10. If the signaling does not settle it, an endpoint sends its highest version, ignores Hellos with a higher unsupported version, and drops down to the highest version it shares. Endpoints SHOULD NOT support versions earlier than 1.10.

For the Diffie-Hellman type, both sides drop choices the other lacks, compare the first item of each list and pick the faster one. The speed ranking from fastest to slowest is DH-2048, ECDH-256, DH-3072, ECDH-384, ECDH-521. In the RFC's example, Alice prefers DH3k and Bob prefers EC25, so both choose EC25. This lets each side start its DH computation as soon as it sees the Hello. All other algorithms are whatever the initiator picks from those in common.

If both sides send a Commit at once, ties are broken by rule. A DH Commit beats a Preshared one. Between two Preshared Commits, the side that is not a PBX (no M flag) becomes the initiator. Between two DH or two non-DH Commits, the Commit with the lowest hvi or nonce value is discarded, comparing them as large unsigned integers.
sections.plainLanguage: Both phones list their favorite locks. They pick the fastest lock they both own, and if they both shout "I'll go first" at once, a simple number comparison decides who does.

sections.title: Packets and Messages
sections.content:
Every ZRTP packet starts with the bits 0001, then 12 unused bits, a 16-bit sequence number that starts at a random value, and the magic cookie 0x5a525450, which spells "ZRTP". Next is a Source Identifier (the SSRC of the RTP stream), then the ZRTP message, then a 32-bit CRC as defined for SCTP in RFC 4960. Because the first two bits are zero the packet looks like RTP version 0, which is invalid, so it cannot be mistaken for RTP, and the cookie makes it differ from STUN.

The RFC adds its own CRC rather than trusting the 16-bit UDP checksum, because an undetected error in the DH exchange could look like an active MiTM attack and cause a false alarm. A packet that fails the CRC is silently discarded.

The Hello message carries version 1.10, a client identifier, hash image H3, the ZID, three flags and lists of hash, cipher, authentication tag, key agreement and SAS types. The flags are S (signature-capable), M (a device such as a PBX that can send SASrelay) and P (passive, never sends Commit). All endpoints MUST support SHA-256, AES-128, HMAC-SHA1 tags of 32 and 80 bits, DH3k and the base32 SAS type.
sections.plainLanguage: Every ZRTP packet starts with a special stamp that says "this is ZRTP, not music", and ends with a check number to catch any scribbles made on the way.

sections.title: Authenticating the Exchange
sections.content:
Diffie-Hellman alone is open to a man-in-the-middle, so ZRTP adds three defenses. First, the initiator sends a hash commitment (hvi) to its public value in the Commit message, before seeing the responder's value. This leaves an attacker only one guess at matching the SAS, so the SAS can be short: a 16-bit SAS gives the attacker one chance in 65536 of avoiding detection.

Second, both users read the Short Authentication String aloud. With the base32 type, the leftmost 20 bits become four characters; with the base256 type, the leftmost 16 bits become two words from the PGP Word List. The comparison must be done with a live human at the other end, because a robot voice can be forged by a MiTM. A mismatch signals an attack. The SAS may also be authenticated by an optional digital signature sent in the Confirm messages.

Third, key continuity. Each endpoint caches shared secrets, indexed by the peer's ZID, and mixes them into later calls. A MiTM would have to have been present from the first call, and the cache is refreshed every call, so a stolen cache gives an attacker only one chance, in the very next session. The RFC calls this self-healing. The SAS Verified flag (V) records that a user already compared the SAS, so it need not be repeated.
sections.plainLanguage: The phones lock in their guess before seeing each other's, so a cheater cannot adjust. Then the friends read a short word code to each other, and they remember a secret for next time.

sections.title: Signaling, Attacks and Intermediaries
sections.content:
ZRTP defends against injected packets with a one-way hash chain. Each side picks a random 256-bit H0 and computes H1 = hash(H0), H2 = hash(H1), H3 = hash(H2). H3 goes in Hello, H2 in Commit, H1 in DHPart1 or DHPart2, and H0 in the Confirm messages. A recipient hashes each value and checks it against the earlier one, rejecting false packets cheaply before any expensive DH work. The responder also rejects a public value equal to 1 or p-1.

In SIP, the a=zrtp-hash SDP attribute carries a hash of the whole Hello message, tying the media to the signaling and letting false Hellos be rejected. If the signaling has end-to-end integrity protection, the hash chain MACs authenticate the whole key exchange, so MiTM protection works even without comparing the SAS.

For intermediaries, the RECOMMENDED behavior is to pass ZRTP through transparently. Back-to-back ZRTP through a middlebox is NOT RECOMMENDED and will always trigger a MiTM alarm, except for a trusted PBX. The Disclosure flag (D) lets a product that deliberately discloses session keys, such as for call monitoring, say so to the other party. The RFC states there are no back doors in the protocol itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message carries a link from a chain that only the real sender could have made, so strangers' fake messages are spotted quickly. A product that shares your key with someone must admit it.

fields.desc: Set to 0001, which looks like invalid RTP version 0 to RTP receivers.

fields.name: Not Used
fields.desc: Set to zero and ignored on receipt.

fields.desc: Incremented per ZRTP packet, starting from a random value.

fields.desc: SSRC of the RTP stream this packet relates to.

fields.desc: Variable length, depending on the message type.

fields.desc: 32-bit CRC over the packet, as in RFC 4960.
